english.html: professors of such ravings boast that they can procure spirits, and by their juggleries and illusions do all things, even to drawing down the stars from heaven; witness Virgil, when he says <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>:

notes.citation: Virgil, Eclogues 8.69 (printed "the thirteenth of the Aeneid", which has twelve books; the line is from the eighth Eclogue)
notes.gloss: Carmina vel caelo possunt deducere lunam: charms can draw the moon down from the sky.

notes.original: Carmina, Vel cœlo poſſunt deducere Lunam.
notes.gloss: Translated in the text with the Latin in parentheses; the print's capital V on Vel is a sort for the verse.

english.html: Charms can even draw down the Moon from heaven (Carmina vel coelo possunt deducere Lunam).

Of this magic some make two kinds, Goety and Theurgy; others (as Marcus Varro) four: Necromancy, Pyromancy, Aeromancy and Hydromancy i. The more recent add to these four Geomancy and Chiromancy k. Necromancy and Goety are all one, signifying the art of divining by the invocation of the spirits of the dead: called Necromancy from νεκρός, which means dead, and μαντεία, divination l; and Goety from planctus (wailing), for the mourning that must be made about the sepulchre from which one wishes to draw and invoke the shade m. Or else, and most often, this pernicious art is practised by the invocation of unclean and evil spirits: as when Pharaoh's enchanters turned rods into serpents and the waters of the rivers into blood n, and the Pythoness of Endor, at the request of King Saul, made the soul of Samuel come by her familiar spirit o — for, as many interpret, it was not the soul of the Prophet, but of some evil spirit which had taken his form p, or else a spectre or phantom. From Goety Theurgy differs in this, that Theurgy is practised by invocation of God and of the good spirits, such as the Angels; by which, by means of the abstinences and other ceremonies required, many have thought they could draw to themselves the celestial powers and divine virtues: which is attributed to Apollonius of Tyana, of whom marvellous things are related — namely, that he understood the jargon of birds; could tell all that was being done in the strangest and most far-removed countries of the world; spoke all tongues without ever having been taught; declared the thoughts of men; foretold things to come; and (what is above all astonishing [the print has amiable, read as admirable], and what a Christian ought not easily to believe) raised the dead — which he boasted he did by the counsel of God and the

notes.citation: Marcus Terentius Varro (Marc Varron), Antiquitates rerum divinarum, book VII as cited (the work is lost; the four kinds of divination by the elements — geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, pyromancy — are reported from Varro by Augustine, City of God VII.35)
notes.original: M. Varro au vij. diuinarum rerũ.
notes.gloss: Coras's "necromancy" in place of Varro's "geomancy" follows Augustine's remark in the same chapter that the dead too were consulted.

notes.citation: Polydore Vergil (Polidore), De inventoribus rerum I.23 (as cited; chapter unverified)
notes.original: Polidore au liure j. de Inuentor. rer. c. xxiij.
notes.gloss: Polydore Vergil of Urbino, 1470–1555; his first book treats the origins of divination and magic.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 26 q. 5, the last canon (c. Nec mirum, c. 14)
notes.gloss: The canon's etymology of necromantia from the Greek for the dead and for divination, which Coras repeats.

notes.citation: Augustine, City of God, book X, chapters 9, 10 and 11 (the book number is not printed; book X is the one that treats goety and theurgy, with Porphyry's doubts)
notes.original: S. Auguſtin au liure de ciuit. Dei. c. ix. x. & xj.
notes.gloss: Augustine, De civitate Dei X.9, the "detestable" arts called goety by the vulgar and theurgy by their defenders.
Pharaoh's magicians turn rods into serpents and water into blood.

notes.citation: 1 Kings 28 (the Vulgate's first book of Kings; 1 Samuel 28 in the Hebrew numbering): the woman of Endor and Samuel
notes.original: Au premier des Rois c. xxviij.

notes.citation: Decretum, C. 26 q. 5, the last canon (c. Nec mirum, c. 14), at § Praeterea (paragraph not verified)
notes.original: c. fi. P. præterea. xxvj. q. v.
notes.gloss: For the interpretation that it was a demon in Samuel's shape, not the prophet's soul — the view of many Fathers, which Augustine weighed both ways. The print's P. is its sort for §.
